Sumimi v0.5.2 — **the reports were counting too much, and the three engines
are now one implementation**.

v0.5.0 brought the marked traffic (the bots) into the reports. The condition
that leaves it out was missing a pair of parentheses, and `AND` binds tighter
than `OR` — so the condition became

```sql
website_id = ? AND created_at >= ? AND created_at < ? AND tag IS NULL
  OR (tag <> ? AND tag <> ? AND …)
```

which SQL reads as *(… and the row is not marked) **or** (the row is not marked
by any of the other kinds)*. The second half has no website and no time in it,
so **every unmarked row in the database was counted**, whatever site it belonged
to and whatever day it was from.

⇒ ⇒ The visitor and the session counts were too big — a month that holds 917
visitors reported 1530, and a window that holds nothing reported the whole
site's traffic. The page view count was right (it is filtered by the same
clause but counted per row), the **breaddowns** were wrong the same way, and
the **marked traffic was never left out** — the clause that was supposed to
exclude it was the clause that let everything else in.

**It is fixed, and the fix is a pair of parentheses.**

---

## One: the condition is bracketed

`service/src/query.rs` — the clause the marked traffic is left out by is now
one condition among the others:

```sql
website_id = ? AND created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?
  AND (tag IS NULL OR (tag <> ? AND tag <> ? AND …))
```

Every report reads the same clause now: the summary, the breakdowns, the time
series, the event log, the revenue.

---

## Two: one implementation, three engines

The bug above is the kind that only a **copy** produces. The reports were
written down three times — once for DuckDB, once for SQLite, and once for
PostgreSQL in the private repository — and the copies had drifted: the
PostgreSQL one was still counting the visitors the way v9 counted them, was
still anchoring a session's length on the eight-byte identifier of v8 (SQL
that does not run against a UUID at all), was reading microseconds as if they
were seconds in the time series, was querying a `tag` column the `revenue`
table does not have, and never left the marked traffic out at all.

⇒ ⇒ So the three copies are now **one**:

| what | where it lives now |
|---|---|
| the columns of the tables | `service/src/schema.rs` — one list, each engine spells it (`Types`) |
| the statements of the reports | `service/src/query.rs` — one set, each engine says how it spells things (`Dialect`) |
| the reading of a row | `service/src/row.rs` — one mapping, **by column name** |
| the dataset and the numbers it computes for itself | `service/src/testing/` — the truth, in the open repository |

An engine now says five things and nothing else: its placeholder (`?`, `?1`,
`$1`), how a moment becomes microseconds, how the larger of two values is
spelled, how a number with a fraction is cast, and how a moment falls into its
bucket.

**By column name** is the part worth keeping: a row read by position is a row
read by a number somebody has to remember, and adding a column moves every
number after it. The PostgreSQL backend was reading the event's type where the
tag was, and the tag where the data was — and nothing complained, because the
report answered.

---

## Three: the truth moved to the open repository

The conformance suite — the one that computes the expected numbers **in plain
Rust**, so that a backend is measured against the truth and not against
another backend — lived in the private repository. It is the suite that found
the parenthesis bug (both open-source engines had it, so every cross-backend
test passed while the numbers were wrong).

⇒ ⇒ It is in `service/src/testing/` now, and the open-source engines are
measured against it too.

---

## What this release costs

Nothing to migrate: **schema v10 is unchanged** — the tables are the same
tables, and an instance that is already on v10 needs no migration.

The numbers change: the visitor, session and breakdown counts of every report
that has more than one website or more than one window in the database were
too big, and are now the numbers the truth says.

**The PostgreSQL backend is a private edition**; there is nothing to download
for it here. What changed for it is the same change: it now runs the same
statements as the other two engines, and its numbers agree with theirs.
